provisions_triggered.name: Due Process / Law of the Land

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the findings that the child was deprived, that the causes and conditions of deprivation were likely to continue, and that continued deprivation would probably cause serious harm were each supported by clear and convincing evidence and were not clearly erroneous.
key_cases.relevance: States North Dakota's three-element termination test and the clear-and-convincing burden carried by the petitioning agency.
key_cases.quote: termination of parental rights requires satisfaction of a three-pronged test which the party petitioning for termination must prove by clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination of an incarcerated father's parental rights, holding incarceration alone does not prove abandonment but prognostic evidence of a long-continuing inability to care for the children satisfied both the state clear-and-convincing standard and ICWA's beyond-a-reasonable-doubt requirement.
key_cases.relevance: Governs termination cases involving an incarcerated parent: imprisonment alone is not abandonment, but prognostic evidence of prolonged inability to parent will support termination.
key_cases.quote: While incarceration, by itself, does not establish abandonment of a child for purposes of terminating parental rights

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed termination, holding the juvenile court correctly applied the law and that clear and convincing evidence supported findings of deprivation, likely continuation of the causes of deprivation, resulting harm, and reasonable reunification efforts.
key_cases.relevance: Restates that each statutory element of termination must be proven by clear and convincing evidence.
key_cases.quote: These elements must be established by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of H.G.C.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed an order terminating a father's parental rights for abandonment under N.D.C.C. § 14-15-19(3)(a) in connection with a stepparent adoption, holding the district court's abandonment findings were not clearly erroneous.
key_cases.relevance: Supplies the abandonment ground by which parental rights may be terminated inside an adoption action, without a dependency case.
key_cases.quote: A parent's intent to abandon may be inferred from the parent's conduct.

key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that before a State may irrevocably terminate parental rights, due process requires proof by at least clear and convincing evidence, striking down New York's fair-preponderance standard.
key_cases.relevance: Federal constitutional floor for the burden of proof in every termination of parental rights case.
key_cases.quote: due process requires that the State support its allegations by at least clear and convincing evidence

key_cases.case_name: Lassiter v. Department of Social Services of Durham County
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Court held that due process does not automatically require appointed counsel for an indigent parent in every termination proceeding; the trial court decides the question case by case under the Eldridge factors, subject to appellate review, and no counsel was constitutionally required on these facts.
key_cases.relevance: Sets the federal floor on appointed counsel in termination cases, which state statutes may and often do exceed.
key_cases.quote: there is a right to appointed counsel only where the indigent, if he is unsuccessful, may lose his personal freedom

key_cases.case_name: In the Matter of the Adoption of S.R.F.
key_cases.holding: The court affirmed a judgment terminating a mother's parental rights for abandonment under N.D.C.C. §§ 14-15-06(1)(a) and 14-15-19(3)(a) and granting the guardians' adoption petition, holding the abandonment findings were not clearly erroneous and overruling prior cases that had applied de novo review to adoption-act appeals.
key_cases.relevance: This is the abandonment authority Adoption of H.G.C. quotes: it sets out the factors — contact and communication, love and affection, intent, and acceptance of parental obligations — and fixes the clear-and-convincing burden for terminating rights inside an adoption action.
key_cases.quote: A party seeking termination of the parent-child relationship in the context of an adoption proceeding must prove the elements necessary to support termination by clear and convincing evidence.

key_cases.holding: The court affirmed the denial of a mother's motion to withdraw her consent to termination of her parental rights, holding the motion was untimely because N.D.C.C. § 27-20-45(6) bars any challenge to a termination order more than thirty days after it is issued by a person who did not retain custody of the child.
key_cases.relevance: Governs the voluntary route to termination: once a parent consents and the order issues, a thirty-day statutory bar forecloses reopening it on any ground, including fraud, unless the parent retained custody.
key_cases.quote: The mother's motion was untimely under N.D.C.C. § 27-20-45(6) and the juvenile court did not err in denying the mother's motion to withdraw her consent.

key_cases.holding: The court retained jurisdiction and remanded with instructions to issue a new order based only on the trial evidence, holding that even when the statutory elements of N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c) are established the juvenile court retains discretion whether to terminate, and that it abused that discretion by relying on evidence outside the record and on a clearly erroneous count of the child's nights in foster care.
key_cases.relevance: Current-chapter authority: it lays out both grounds under N.D.C.C. § 27-20.3-20(1)(c) — likely-to-continue need for protection with resulting harm, and 450 of the previous 660 nights in foster care — and holds the decision to terminate is discretionary even once a ground is proven.
key_cases.quote: Therefore, when the statutory elements to terminate parental rights are met, the court has discretion, but is not required, to terminate parental rights.
